findings.summary: The suppression guard around `sequencer.close()` catches `IOException` only, while the field it suppresses onto is deliberately a `Throwable`. The comment 45 lines above (line 402-407) argues exactly why the narrow type is wrong -- "`Throwable`, not `IOException`, and the difference is reachable: an UncheckedIOException out of the flush would leave an IOException-typed field null and the release failure would replace it -- the same masking, one type narrower" -- and then the catch on the release side is written one type narrower. The adjacent claim "SUPPRESSED, NEVER SUBSTITUTED" (line 442) is therefore absolute where the code is conditional. `Sequencer.close()` declares only IOException, but it is an interface with a decorator already in the tree (`IngestCommitPathTest.Recording`) and a remote implementation coming in M5, and the release path bottoms out in `BinStore.putIfMatch`, which no gate stops an SDK-backed backend from throwing unchecked out of.
findings.failure_scenario: A pod shuts down while the store is failing. flushNow() throws -- the final segment is lost -- and the release then throws an unchecked exception (an SDK RuntimeException out of putIfMatch, an IllegalStateException from a closed HTTP client, or a decorating Sequencer's own bug). It escapes the `finally` uncaught, replaces the flush failure, and the operator is told the lease could not be released by a pod that just lost its last segment: the round-1 defect, on the one path the new guard does not cover. Widening to `catch (Throwable)` (or `RuntimeException | IOException`) would close it and match the field's declared type.

findings.summary: The SURVIVING HALF of round-1 finding 1, whose failure_scenario named both halves. `drainPushes()` re-asserts the current thread's interrupt flag when its `pusher.join` is interrupted (line 486-489: `Thread.currentThread().interrupt();`), and `sequencer.close()` is called immediately after it on the same thread. The release path is interruptible: LeaseManager.release -> BoundedLock.takeOrFail -> `lock.tryLock(bound, NANOSECONDS)` throws InterruptedException at once when the flag is set, and BoundedLock converts it to `IOException("interrupted waiting for the lease lock to release")`. So on an interrupted shutdown the release is not merely reported as failed -- it is never attempted, and the lease is left to lapse. The masking half is genuinely fixed; the ordering half is not, and nothing in the new comment block constrains the position beyond "AFTER the final flush", which `sequencer.close()` before `drainPushes()` would also satisfy.
findings.failure_scenario: A shutdown hook or supervisor thread calling close() is interrupted (a Kubernetes grace-period racer, a JUnit timeout in the plugin ITs, an executor shutdownNow in the wiring commit). The final flush succeeds, drainPushes' join is interrupted and re-sets the flag, and the release fails instantly without touching the store. The successor waits out the full lease TTL -- ADR-0007's ~10 s -- which is precisely the cost this commit spends one extra conditional PUT and moves a cost assertion from 4 to 5 to buy. The failure is reported as "a store call is still in flight", which is false, so the message points an operator at the store rather than at the interrupt.

findings.summary: close() now closes a collaborator it did not create, and that ownership transfer is documented ONLY inside the method body. The constructor (line 137) has no javadoc at all, `close()` has no javadoc, and `Ingest`'s own contract says nothing about the sequencer -- so nothing a caller reads before passing a Sequencer says the ingester will release its lease. The decision itself is sanctioned by the task row; what is missing is its statement on the public surface, and the next row in the backlog is the one that will get this wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.17 adds the renew tick the backlog now owns. The obvious wiring builds one LocalSequencer, hands it to DefaultIngest and gives the same instance to the ticker (or to a supervisor that recreates the ingester on a config change). The first ingester close() releases the lease underneath both; the ticker's next renew() sees belief == null, reads that as fenced, and the pod stands down or burns an epoch re-acquiring -- and the code that caused it is a constructor argument whose javadoc never said it was consumed. One sentence on the constructor and on close() ("this ingester OWNS the sequencer and releases it on close") is the whole fix.

findings.summary: The edited hunk keeps a clause that its own new text and another javadoc in the same file contradict: "{@code CONTINUE} may not use {@code prevEpoch=0} as a \"no previous chain\" sentinel, because 0 now names a live one". `CommitLog.open`'s javadoc (line 295-299) states the opposite as a settled choice -- "{@code prevEpoch == 0} is not a placeholder. Epoch 0 is RESERVED for the unleased chain (M4.4b), so a first leader naming it says truthfully that there was no predecessor chain -- which M4.5 chose over an explicit absent-marker" -- and `LocalSequencer.start` does exactly that on every first term (`prevEpoch = epoch - 1` = 0 at epoch 1, then `log.open(prevEpoch, prevSeq)`), with ChainReplay terminating its crossing at `chainEpoch >= 1`. This commit is what resolves the disagreement (it is now safe BECAUSE nothing in production writes epoch 0), and the same sentence the author rewrote is where the stale half survives. Round-1's major 2 was this defect class -- a load-bearing comment false at its named exemplar -- so the standard here is not "harmless prose".
findings.failure_scenario: A reader reconciling the two javadocs at M4.6f or M4.8 concludes that LocalSequencer.start's `open(0, 0)` at epoch 1 is the sentinel misuse the class javadoc forbids, and either 'fixes' it (changing a wire value in CONTINUE, which is a wire-format change with no ADR) or, reading it the other way, assumes a first leader DOES inherit from an epoch-0 chain and so does not notice that offsets from a real M1-era epoch-0 chain are dropped on the first leased term. Both readings are available from the same paragraph.

notes: ROUND-1 FINDINGS, verified individually. r1-1 (release masking the final flush) FIXED, and fixed with a test that discriminates: aFailedLeaseReleaseIsSuppressedRatherThanReplacingAFailedFinalFlush asserts the propagating exception has a non-empty getSuppressed(), which fails if the release substitutes. The Throwable+catch+rethrow shape is sound on every path I traced: flush succeeds (flushFailure null, a failing release propagates on its own); flush throws checked or unchecked or Error (caught by catch(Throwable), rethrown by precise rethrow which types as IOException|RuntimeException|Error, so close()'s throws clause still holds, and the release rides suppressed); double close is safe (flushNow finds pending empty and returns; drainPushes' POISON lands on a dead pusher and join returns immediately; LocalSequencer.close sets closed then LeaseManager.release returns before any I/O because belief == null after the first release, so no second request and no throw); self-suppression is impossible since flushFailure and releaseFailed are distinct objects. Two residues, both filed above as minors: the catch is narrower than the field (r2-1) and the interrupt-flag ordering r1-1 already named (r2-2). r1-2 (false justification) FIXED and the replacements CHECKED rather than trusted: DefaultIngestTest has exactly five request-delta assertions over CountingBinStore reading isEqualTo(4) (lines 83, 254, 326, 345, 420) and IngestShutdownTest one isEqualTo(5) (line 76); IntervalPutRateTest names no Sequencer, no CommitLog and no DefaultIngest, and its javadoc line 35-39 says verbatim what TestSequencers now quotes; nothing under http/src/test reads counts() (grep is empty); http/build.gradle.kts and plugin/build.gradle.kts now give the true reason. r1-3 DEFERRED to M4.18 and the deferral is safe: every call site in the tree passes the same store and prefix to both, so the tree is correct today and the hazard is a future wiring commit. r1-4 DEFERRED to M4.17, liveness only, and unreachable today because nothing wires DefaultIngest in production; LocalSequencer.commit never consults the lease, so the http/plugin fixtures outliving the 10 s TTL cannot flake either. r1-5 DEFERRED to M4.10, safe because nothing reads podId or flushSeq yet and the increment is before the commit, so a failed or ambiguous flush consumes a key rather than reusing one -- the safe direction. r1-6 FIXED: M4.6f now sits at backlog line 259, immediately after M4.6d and ahead of M4.7-M4.15. COST, judged not assumed: per-flush requests are unchanged (sequencer.commit delegates to the same log.commit, one conditional PUT); the only new steady-state request is one putIfMatch per DefaultIngest.close(), i.e. once per pod lifetime, scaling with nodes and not with records, shards, partitions or indices; the 4->5 assertion is an exact equality, not a relaxed bound, and is argued in the test rather than quietly bumped. Recovery moving out of the constructor adds nothing: it is the same LIST+GET walk, now in LocalSequencer.start, and the per-restart lease/seal/CONTINUE cost is M4.6e's already-recorded and already-pinned growth. FILE TRIM: nothing load-bearing was deleted to get under 500 lines. The 12-line startup-latency block removed from the constructor already exists verbatim at LocalSequencer.java:97-108 (added by M4.6e, not by this diff), and the only other deletion is closeFlushesWhatIsStillBufferedRatherThanLosingIt, which reappears in IngestShutdownTest with identical assertions apart from the argued 4->5. DefaultIngest.java is now 495 lines, 5 under the gate. NO POST-CLOSE COMMIT: flushLoop evaluates its loop condition only while holding the lock that close() sets `closed` under, so every sequencer.commit strictly precedes sequencer.close(). WORKING TREE, not a finding against the staged bytes but worth knowing before committing: sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/LocalSequencer.java carries an UNSTAGED mutation (`new CommitLog(store, prefix, epoch + 1)` at line 96) and ingest/src/test/java/binjava/ingest/IngestCommitPathTest.java an unstaged `// MUTANT: no append at all` at line 55 -- both appeared during this review and look like a falsifiability experiment in flight. Neither is in the diff I reviewed; both would be wrong to commit.
